title: Dispersion and Index Numbers
lines: Two classes can have the same mean mark and still be very different: in one everyone scores near 60, in the other marks run from 20 to 100. Dispersion measures this spread. USAT asks you to compute the range, quartile deviation, mean deviation, variance and standard deviation from small data sets, to compare groups with the coefficient of variation, to judge skewness, and to work simple index numbers.
## Absolute and relative measures
Absolute measures carry the units of the data (kg, rupees). Relative measures, or coefficients, have no units and let you compare groups measured differently.
| Absolute | Relative (coefficient)
| Range = xₘ − x₀ | (xₘ − x₀) ÷ (xₘ + x₀)
| Q.D. = (Q₃ − Q₁)/2 | (Q₃ − Q₁) ÷ (Q₃ + Q₁)
| M.D. = Σ|x − x̄| ÷ n | M.D. ÷ mean
## Quartiles, deciles and percentiles

Quartiles cut ordered data into four equal parts, deciles into ten and percentiles into a hundred. For raw data Q₁ is the ((n + 1)/4)th value and Q₃ the (3(n + 1)/4)th value. For grouped data use Q₁ = L + (h/f)(n/4 − C), like the median formula. Useful equalities: Q₂ = D₅ = P₅₀ = median, and D₇ = P₇₀.
## Variance and standard deviation
Variance σ² is the mean of the squared deviations; S.D. σ is its positive square root. A shortcut avoids working out each deviation:
- σ² = Σx²/n − (Σx/n)².
- Adding a constant changes nothing; multiplying by a multiplies σ by |a| and σ² by a². So Var(ax + b) = a²·Var(x).
- σ is never negative and is 0 only when all values are equal. M.D. ≤ S.D. always.
- For a normal distribution, Q.D. ≈ ⅔σ and M.D. ≈ ⅘σ.
> Example 1. For 10 values, Σx = 50 and Σx² = 410. Find σ.
> σ² = 41 − 5² = 16, so σ = 4. Stopping at 16 gives the variance, not the S.D.
> Example 2. Ali's mean is 40 runs with S.D. 8; Usman's mean is 50 with S.D. 12. Who is more consistent?
> C.V. for Ali = 20 %, for Usman = 24 %. The lower C.V. wins, so Ali is more consistent.
## Moments, skewness and kurtosis
- The rth moment about the mean is mᵣ = Σ(x − x̄)ʳ ÷ n. m₁ = 0 and m₂ = variance. From moments about any origin, m₂ = m₂′ − (m₁′)².
- Pearson's coefficient of skewness: Sk = (mean − mode) ÷ σ, or 3(mean − median) ÷ σ.
- Bowley's coefficient: (Q₃ + Q₁ − 2Q₂) ÷ (Q₃ − Q₁), which lies between −1 and +1.
- Positive Sk: long tail to the right, mean above median. Negative Sk: long tail to the left.
- Kurtosis is peakedness, measured by b₂ = m₄ ÷ m₂². Normal (mesokurtic) b₂ = 3; more peaked is leptokurtic; flatter is platykurtic.
> Example 3. Mean 30, median 27, σ = 6. Pearson's Sk = 3(30 − 27) ÷ 6 = 1.5, a positive skew.
## Index numbers
An index number shows the change in a price or quantity compared with a base period set at 100.
- Price relative = (p₁ ÷ p₀) × 100. An index of 125 means a 25 % rise.
- Simple aggregative index = Σp₁ ÷ Σp₀ × 100 (no weights).
- Laspeyres = Σp₁q₀ ÷ Σp₀q₀ × 100 (base-year quantities).
- Paasche = Σp₁q₁ ÷ Σp₀q₁ × 100 (current-year quantities).
- Fisher's ideal index = √(Laspeyres × Paasche).
- Chain base: link relative = (pₙ ÷ pₙ₋₁) × 100; chain index = previous chain index × link relative ÷ 100.
- A consumer price index measures the cost of living. Real wage = money wage × 100 ÷ CPI.
- Shifting the base: new index = old index ÷ old index of the new base year × 100.
> Example 4. Rice: p₀ = 50, p₁ = 60, q₀ = 10. Sugar: p₀ = 100, p₁ = 105, q₀ = 4. Laspeyres index?
! Var(2x + 5) is 4 × Var(x), not 2 × Var(x) + 5. Constants never change spread.
! Read the stem for the divisor. Descriptive questions divide by n; dividing by n − 1 gives a different variance.
! Percentage changes in a chain compound: rises of 10 % and 20 % give 132, not 130.
## Quick check
- Find the coefficient of range when the largest value is 80 and the smallest 20.
- If σ = 3, what is the variance of 4x − 7?
- Which index uses current-year quantities as weights?
- An index is 90. What happened to prices compared with the base year?
